prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, enabling frequency measurements at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a measurement invention in the literal sense: magic-wavelength trapping lets thousands of atoms be interrogated at once without perturbing the clock transition, so the statistical advantage of an ensemble is combined with the small systematic shifts of a trapped single ion. The result is fractional systematic uncertainties near 1e-18, comparisons between independent labs and across continents, and a clock that resolves gravitational redshift across millimetres. That is a new way of observing nature, with uses already demonstrated or under way in tests of constant variation, dark-matter searches, relativistic geodesy and the coming redefinition of the second. The experimental chain is clean and verifiable: Katori's concept and first Sr lattice clock, then the Ye group's stability and accuracy work, then reproduction at JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, NIST, SYRTE, PTB and elsewhere, with agreement between different atomic species. Two names map onto proposal-plus-first-demonstration and record-precision realisation, which is the cleanest attribution on the shortlist. Unlike several other candidates, nothing about the interpretation is still being debated.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that precision-frequency metrology has been honoured repeatedly (Hall and Hansch in 2005 for the comb, Wineland and Haroche in 2012 for single-quantum-system control), and a committee may read a lattice-clock prize as a further increment on that line rather than a new discovery. The practical payoff, the SI redefinition, has not yet happened, and the fundamental-physics results so far are limits rather than discoveries. Credit is also not airtight: Lemonde's group (SYRTE), Takamoto's early Sr work and the Ludlow and Bloom contributions are all real, and the three-person cap does not leave room for them. Finally, I am a close reader of this field and may rate precision above breadth; the topological-insulator and circuit-QED candidates have strong claims to opening larger intellectual areas.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the lattice clock first because theory and experiment agree quantitatively and the invention opens new measurements, and sees the 2005 and 2012 prizes as neighbouring ground rather than the same invention.
responses.response: I agree, and the strongest version of the argument is about what the instrument measures: relativistic redshift over millimetres and 1e-18 comparisons between species were not accessible with comb-referenced single-ion clocks. I would add one point on maturity that her note leaves implicit. Agreement between independent lattice clocks at this level, including between different atoms, is what separates this from a single-lab result. Where I would qualify her view is the priority history: Katori's proposal and the Takamoto demonstration came before the Ye group's record work, so the citation should name the invention and the realisation, not only the precision race.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as the standard architecture of superconducting quantum processors and the natural successor to the 2025 prize, while flagging his own proximity to that community. He ranks the lattice clock second.
responses.response: I take the architecture argument seriously and it is why I keep B006 as my first alternative; the 2004 strong-coupling experiment and the resulting dispersive readout are real, reproduced and enabling. My reservation is configuration. A four-name proposal (Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin, Schoelkopf) cannot be cut to three without leaving out someone with a strong claim, and the Devoret and transmon lineage sits close to the 2025 laureates, so the novelty relative to 2025 needs to be argued, not assumed. By contrast the clock candidate has a two-name core that does not need defending against its own omissions. I would also ask whether the recognised discovery is the platform or the physics: I find the case for the physics (strong coupling in a one-dimensional resonator) stronger than the case for the processors.

responses.point: Olsson ranks topological insulators first and the lattice clock second, noting that Ye already shares the 2005 prize and that the committee may want to wait for the SI second redefinition.
responses.response: I would correct the factual premise: as I recall it, the 2005 prize went to Glauber, Hall and Hansch, and Ye, who was in Hall's group, was not a laureate. If the committee's records say otherwise, this should be checked before it enters the discussion. On waiting for the redefinition, I disagree: the science does not depend on the legal definition of the second, and the clocks' performance is already verified in many labs. Waiting would tie recognition to a metrology-community decision on timing.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks Kane, Mele and Molenkamp first on the strength of a verified theory-to-experiment chain, a stable interpretation after fifteen-plus years, and a new class of matter.
responses.response: I share his criterion of a verified theory-to-experiment chain and I do not dispute the physics or the timeliness. My reservations are about attribution and overlap, and he states them himself: the HgTe proposal (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang) and the three-dimensional discovery sit outside the credited trio, and the 2016 prize on topological phases covers adjacent ground. A topological-insulator prize with a defensible citation might need to choose between the 2D quantum spin Hall effect and the 3D case. I would regard this as my strongest competitor from outside my own field, and would want condensed-matter colleagues to say whether the three-name configuration is credible.

uncertainties: Whether the committee views a lattice-clock prize as a distinct invention from the precision metrology recognised in 2005 and 2012, or as a continuation of it.
How much weight to give the pending SI redefinition of the second as a maturity argument.
Whether Lemonde, Takamoto or Ludlow have claims strong enough to displace Ye or to merit three names; I recall priority details from memory and have not verified them.
Whether B038 can be given a defensible three-name configuration without the HgTe proposal and the 3D discovery.
statement.conflict_note: I spent part of my doctoral period in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Ye is Hall's former postdoc and a JILA colleague, so there is a personal-scientific proximity to the Ye group that may require recusal or at least disclosure. My own work on spectral-hole-burning crystals and slow-light laser stabilisation touches ultrastable lasers used for clocks, though I have no joint credited work with Katori or Ye apparent from my profile. My WACQT role overlaps institutionally with Chalmers and therefore with Johansson, which is relevant if circuit QED is discussed.
